links.note: The chariot ride on which Siddhartha first saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a composed ascetic - this concept's four sights, and the reason he gave up palace life.
Avidya, ignorance, and attachment as the root causes of suffering - what this concept says he realised under the pipal tree at Bodh Gaya.
What the Jataka tales are - stories of the Buddha's former births expressing Buddhist values in simple terms - is how this concept introduces them at its close.
The Charvaka school, sometimes called Lokayata, holding that this material world is the only thing that exists and that there can therefore be no life after death - this concept's account of it.

A tribe as a group of families or clans sharing common descent, culture and language, living as a close-knit community under a chief and holding no private property - this concept's definition. Already linked and correct.

How anthropologists' view of tribes changed - this concept opens on 19th century anthropologists describing them as primitive or inferior and on those biased judgments being mostly abandoned after deeper study.
Mountains, rivers, trees, plants and animals held sacred in tribal and Hindu belief alike because there is consciousness behind them - this concept's explanation of why the two interact so naturally.
Veda from the Sanskrit vid, meaning knowledge - this concept's etymology. Already linked and correct.
What Nachiketa learns from Yama, that the atman hidden within all creatures is neither born nor dies and is immortal - this concept's telling of the Katha Upanishad story. Already linked and correct.

The tree analogy explained through the schools of thought - this concept is where the shared concepts, dharma, karma and rebirth, are explicitly called the trunk of the tree the chapter started with. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.

How the Vedas were preserved and why it is remarkable - this concept states that for 100 to 200 generations they were committed to memory through rigorous training and passed on orally with hardly any alterations. Already linked and correct.
The Vedic worldview through ritam and ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti - this concept defines ritam as truth and order in the cosmos and quotes the hymn. Already linked and correct.
The Upanishads building on Vedic concepts and introducing brahman, atman, rebirth and karma - all four terms are defined in this concept. Already linked and correct.

The monkey-king who let his troop cross on his body and the human king who drew a lesson about rule from it - this concept tells that tale, which is the first half of the question. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.

What the emphasis on dialogue and questioning reveals - this concept holds both examples the answer names, Nachiketa persisting with Yama and Gargi resuming her questions after being told to stop, and it is where the inset's point about the importance of asking questions is made.
The Sangha, a community of bhikshus and bhikshunis who dedicated themselves to practising and spreading his teachings - this concept's account of why his influence spread. Already linked and correct.
Anekantavada as the truth having many aspects and aparigraha as non-possession - this concept defines both. Already linked and correct.
The mantra ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti and Truth as another name for God - both are in this concept, which is what the multi-faith case is built on. Already linked and correct.

The keyed sub-prompt asks what event prompted Siddhartha's quest, and the next asks what he identified as the root causes of suffering - the four sights and avidya with attachment, both in this concept.

A sacred tree with a spirit in it alongside Singbonga the supreme creator - this concept holds both halves, natural elements as sacred and tribal groups also having a concept of a supreme being, with Singbonga named. Already linked and correct.
Uddalaka's clay analogy and the mantra you are That, Shvetaketu - this concept tells that story with both the banyan seed and the pots of clay. Already linked and correct.
